pr.title: [beta] backports
pr.description:
- Change int-to-ptr transmute lowering back to inttoptr rust-lang/rust#147541
- rewrite outlives placeholder constraints to outlives static when handling opaque types rust-lang/rust#147566
- GVN: Invalidate derefs at loop headers rust-lang/rust#147607

pr.author: cuviper

analysis.summary: GVN must invalidate cached dereferences at loop headers because reverse postorder is not topological once loops exist; otherwise a cached deref of a reference can be reused across a back-edge even though the loop body performs an indirect write through an aliasing place. The PR fixes the miscompile by calling state.invalidate_derefs() at every maybe-loop-header and adds both a MIR-pass regression test and a -O run-pass regression test.
analysis.originalLogic: GVN visits blocks in reverse postorder and caches dereferenced values while assuming no statement from a not-yet-processed block can have performed an indirect write. The pass forwards derefs such as `(*val_alias)` based on this cache. The new helper documents the approximation: "A loop header for us is a block which is visited after its predecessor in" post-order, and "This is ok as we mostly need a heuristic."
analysis.incorrectTransformation: Without loop-header invalidation, GVN's deref cache remains live across a loop back-edge. The historically incorrect result is that GVN uses/reuses the dereference of `val_alias` (the regression test checks for `copy (*[[VAL_REF]])`) at the return/loop path even though the loop body writes through `*val`, which aliases `val_alias`. The fixed pass invalidates all derefs before visiting a loop header, so the test instead requires the pre-loop captured value: `[[V:_.*]] = copy (((*[[VAL_REF]]) as V0).0: i32);` and then `[[RET:_*]] = Value::V0(copy [[V]])`, with `// CEHCK-NOT: copy (*[[VAL_REF]]);` after the loop. This is stated by the source comment: "With loops, reverse postorder cannot produce a valid topological order. A statement or terminator from inside the loop, that is not processed yet, may have performed an indirect write."
analysis.inputDomain: MIR functions containing a loop (including self-loops) where a reference is obtained and dereferenced before or at a loop header, and the loop body/back-edge performs an indirect write through a place that aliases that reference's pointee, e.g. `let val_alias: &Value = get(val); ... let Value::V0(v) = *val_alias ...; loop { ... *val = Value::V1; }` with the value of `v` used after the write. Also relevant: enum discriminant loads through such an aliasing reference. The regression test `tests/mir-opt/gvn_loop.rs` uses `//@ test-mir-pass: GVN` and emits `// EMIT_MIR gvn_loop.loop_deref_mut.GVN.diff`; `tests/ui/mir/gvn-loop-miscompile.rs` is `//@ compile-flags: -O` and `//@ run-pass`.
analysis.trigger: A loop whose back-edge/body contains an indirect write through a reference aliasing a place whose dereference GVN has cached, combined with processing the loop header in reverse postorder before that write has been visited. The header is recognized by `loops::maybe_loop_headers`, which inserts a successor into the set when it is not yet visited during postorder traversal, and marks a block visited only after checking its successors to handle self-loops.
preconditions: The MIR CFG contains a cycle/loop with a loop header identified by postorder approximation.
A dereference of a reference/place is cached by GVN at or before the loop header.
The loop body or back-edge performs an indirect write that may modify the cached pointee (for example `*val = Value::V1`).
The cached dereference is otherwise still considered available at a later use/return path.
GVN processes blocks in reverse postorder, which is not a valid topological order when loops are present.
pitfalls: Do not assume reverse postorder is a topological order once loops exist; a not-yet-processed loop-body statement or terminator may have performed an indirect write before the header at runtime.

The write may be indirect through a reference that aliases the reference being dereferenced (`val_alias` aliases `val`), so invalidation must be conservative rather than checking only direct stores to the same local.
Do not conflate this GVN deref-invalidation issue with borrow-checker post-copy overwrite behavior; only the GVN cache across loop headers is at issue here.
The loop-header computation must insert a successor when not yet visited and mark the current block visited only after checking successors, otherwise self-loops (`bb1: goto -> bb1;`) are missed.
Invalidation must occur before visiting the header block's data, so that cached derefs from before the loop are not used in the header processing.
analysis.testStrategy: Add a focused MIR-pass test annotated `//@ test-mir-pass: GVN` that captures an aliasing reference, dereferences it before a loop, performs an indirect write through the original mutable reference inside the loop, and checks via `EMIT_MIR` diff/`CHECK-NOT` that GVN does not emit a post-write `copy (*VAL_REF)` and instead uses the pre-loop captured value. Also add a `-O` `run-pass` regression that constructs an enum, calls a helper returning an aliasing reference, mutates via `*val` inside the loop, and asserts the returned value is the expected pre-write variant. Vary only the presence/absence of the indirect write in the loop to isolate the stale-deref transformation, and include a self-loop case to exercise the visited-after-successors rule.
